claims.artwork_field_or_region: Opening statement and intra-urban temperature band
exact_locators: b04_s01.txt lines 62-64: developed areas can be hotter than nearby rural areas and hotter areas can occur within a city
b04_s11.txt lines 72-75: uneven buildings and pavements versus trees and greenery create intra-urban heat islands; surface and atmospheric heat islands differ
claims.statement_or_derivation: A city can contain hotter and cooler areas; the urban-rural contrast and the within-city contrast are related but distinct scales.
claims.scope_and_limits: Does not assert that every downtown block is hottest or provide a universal ranking of neighborhoods.

exact_locators: b04_s11.txt line 63: U.S. review found daytime urban areas about 1–7°F higher than outlying areas and nighttime about 2–5°F higher
b04_s14.txt line 90 repeats the same ranges
claims.statement_or_derivation: EPA reports U.S. heat-island differences of about 1–7°F by day and 2–5°F at night.
claims.scope_and_limits: Ranges are national source conclusions, not values for a fictional city, not a measured local dataset, and not a license to infer a midpoint.

exact_locators: b04_s11.txt lines 65-70: reduced natural landscapes, material properties, urban geometry, human-generated heat, and weather/geography all contribute
b04_s11.txt line 67: urban materials can absorb and emit more solar heat and release heat slowly after sunset
claims.statement_or_derivation: Urban heat arises from interacting surface, geometry, activity, and weather factors rather than one cause.
claims.scope_and_limits: Diagram is conceptual. Arrow thickness must not be read as measured shares unless a dataset is later added.

exact_locators: b04_s11.txt lines 74-77: surface temperatures vary more during the day; surface and atmospheric heat islands differ
b04_s12.txt lines 82-86 and 100-104: air temperature reflects conditions people experience; surface data has different coverage and limitations
claims.statement_or_derivation: A hot pavement reading and the air temperature at head height answer different questions.
claims.scope_and_limits: No numeric conversion from surface to air temperature will be shown; the sources warn against treating them as interchangeable.

exact_locators: b04_s02.txt lines 56-58: trees and vegetation lower surface and air temperatures through shade and evapotranspiration
b04_s11.txt lines 66-68: vegetation, material properties, and building geometry affect heat
claims.statement_or_derivation: Shade changes exposure while evapotranspiration removes heat from air; street geometry affects airflow and solar access.
claims.scope_and_limits: Street section is explanatory, not a simulation. Cooling depends on species, water, climate, and placement; no universal cooling value is claimed.

exact_locators: b04_s11.txt lines 63 and 67-68: nighttime urban-rural contrast and slow heat release after sunset
b04_s09.txt lines 85-89: HeatRisk considers duration of unusual heat and whether warm overnight lows continue stress
b04_s12.txt line 89: nighttime temperatures can pose higher health risks
claims.statement_or_derivation: Sunset does not immediately remove urban heat; stored heat and warm nights can matter to exposure and health.
claims.scope_and_limits: Timeline is qualitative. It will not invent hourly temperatures or imply that every material releases heat at the same rate.

exact_locators: b04_s02.txt line 69: EPA reports that less-vegetated areas can be hotter and linked to lower-income, Hispanic, and Black residents
b04_s11.txt line 81: heat is of greatest concern for several age, income, occupation, health, disability, and mobility groups
b04_s12.txt lines 65 and 78: assessment can ask where vulnerable populations live in warmer neighborhoods and focus on intra-urban air-temperature hot spots
claims.statement_or_derivation: Cooling access is an equity question because heat exposure and the ability to reach safe cool spaces are unevenly distributed.
claims.scope_and_limits: No invented demographic percentages or local redlining map. This piece must not imply that vegetation alone measures equity or that any group is uniformly vulnerable.

claims.artwork_field_or_region: Heat Index 96°F / 65% RH / feels-like 121°F example and assumptions
exact_locators: b04_s09.txt line 61: NWS example states 96°F air temperature plus 65% relative humidity gives a 121°F heat index
b04_s09.txt line 62: heat index was devised for shade and light wind; full sunshine can increase values by up to 15°F; strong hot dry winds can be hazardous
claims.statement_or_derivation: Heat Index combines air temperature and relative humidity, but its standard assumptions matter.
claims.scope_and_limits: The 121°F value is a source example, not a forecast or a local measurement. The up-to-15°F sunshine note will not be automatically added as if it were a fixed correction.

exact_locators: b04_s09.txt lines 63-66: WBGT includes temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation, and other parameters and can inform activity modification
b04_s09.txt lines 81-89: HeatRisk considers departure from normal, time of year, duration, and heat-health thresholds
claims.statement_or_derivation: Different heat tools answer different exposure and planning questions; Heat Index is not the only relevant measure.
claims.scope_and_limits: The NWS page labels HeatRisk experimental and not supported 24/7; that status will be preserved if mentioned.

exact_locators: b04_s02.txt lines 56-66: shade, evapotranspiration, energy, air quality, and stormwater co-benefits
b04_s03.txt lines 69-86: green roofs provide shade and evapotranspiration; extensive and intensive types differ; green and cool roofs have different strengths
b04_s04.txt lines 64-68: cool roofs use solar reflectance and thermal emittance
b04_s05.txt lines 57-68: cool pavements may reflect solar energy or enhance evaporation and can have stormwater and comfort benefits
b04_s14.txt lines 97-120: multi-strategy approach depends on climate, co-benefits, funding, vulnerability data, and feasibility
claims.statement_or_derivation: Trees, green roofs, cool roofs, and cool pavements operate through different mechanisms and should be selected for local constraints and co-benefits, not reduced to one universal winner.
claims.scope_and_limits: Matrix uses qualitative mechanisms and source-described tradeoffs. It will not rank strategies using incomparable effect sizes.

claims.artwork_field_or_region: Fictional cool-corridor plan and planning prompts
exact_locators: b04_s14.txt lines 114-120: strategy selection depends on climate, co-benefits, funding, vulnerability data, and policy feasibility
b04_s02.txt line 58, b04_s04.txt lines 64-68, b04_s05.txt lines 57-68: mechanisms of shade, reflective roofs, and cooler pavements
claims.statement_or_derivation: A cool-corridor concept can combine connected shade, cooler surfaces, rest points, and measurement to turn isolated interventions into a continuous public-space strategy.
claims.scope_and_limits: The street, measurements, budget, and residents are fictional demonstration content. The corridor is an editorial synthesis, not a source-endorsed plan or a predicted temperature reduction.

exact_locators: b04_s12.txt lines 65-68 and 71-80: define objective, geography, time, season, and air-versus-surface data need
b04_s12.txt lines 94-104: representative sites, enough sites, consistent protocol, metadata, and satellite/air limitations
claims.statement_or_derivation: Credible heat mapping starts with a question, consistent measurements, representative sites, and documented limitations.
claims.scope_and_limits: Guide is a concise editorial adaptation, not a complete field protocol or a claim that community sensors alone produce a representative citywide map.

datasets.denominator: not a ratio; paired regional contrast
datasets.time_range: General U.S. review conclusion reported on the accessed pages; the pages do not state a single observation period in the quoted passage
datasets.processing: Exact range transcription. Draw interval bands only; do not calculate a midpoint or fabricate city-level samples.
datasets.artwork_mapping: Two labelled horizontal interval bands labelled DAY and NIGHT with the qualifier 'about' and 'U.S. source review'.

datasets.unit: degrees Fahrenheit and percent relative humidity
datasets.time_range: Illustrative NWS example, not a time-series observation
datasets.processing: Exact transcription of the worked example. Do not present as a newly calculated forecast. Preserve shade/light-wind assumptions and separate full-sunshine caveat.
datasets.artwork_mapping: Three-part equation-like composition: 96°F AIR + 65% RH → 121°F FEELS LIKE, with assumption card below.

uncertainties.handling: Use a mechanism-and-tradeoff matrix; no aggregate score or universal winner.
